Buckle up because here's a story; some preface, this takes place in 2007-2008 and I was, at the time, no older than 13. Ever since I started the game in 2006 I've had questing, and subsequently lore, as my primary reason to play the game; this being the case, my stats and thus money-making methods until I achieved my goal of all quests completed were very lacking. Come the latter half of 2007 it was announced that a new skill was coming to the game, a feature I was very excited for based on core concepts and of course a skill cape with a wolf icon was a good goal for me at the time. As I mentioned, my money-making methods were severely under-par as I did not engage in boss fights or skill efficiently and my primary source was clue rewards; that is, until I discovered a new money-making method in the wake of trade limits and specific task sets. My new method of making money involved my close-knit group of 5 friends and myself hacking away at the brush on a tropical island looking for a rare item needed for the task sets yet uncommonly brought into the game. Each of these items was worth, at the time, between 500k-1m coins and with proper timing one plant could be harvested by every person present! We made a good chunk of change in the month we did this method, and subsequently I gathered literally thousands of a certain byproduct as a result of our efforts. By the end of December 2007 I had amassed well over 35k of these seemingly useless items with the assumption they were just a pointless byproduct of our gathering; I eventually discarded them sometime before the new skill came out in January 2008. Going by the prices of just today, 35k of those items is worth a significant amount, back then they were worth well over 525m, not to mention the in-game currency value was higher back then.

TL;DR: Amassed 35k "useless" items, discarded them on a whim assuming they'd always be useless, lost out on 525m in-game currency in 2008.

It's akin to why a certain vigilante doesn't resort to lethal measures against the supervillains he consistently apprehends. As with all morals, the interpretation and application of these principles are entirely personal, so I understand why some may have no issues with fighting on the same level, while others find that concept repugnant. In a real-world context, this is why it was agreed upon in the international conventions to refrain from using grossly inhumane tactics in warfare. Conflict occurs; it's inherent to the chaos of existence, but the manner in which war is conducted is a different matter.

One character is portrayed as an extreme example of an antihero in contrast to the main group; she receives less sympathy from those who disapprove of her extremist views, her reasoning understood but not accepted. Another character is depicted as someone unwilling to engage further with either side and grapples with the choice of remaining neutral; her reasoning is relatable, and while her past actions were morally questionable, there is acknowledgment that she recognized her wrongdoing and felt genuine remorse for her actions. A third character serves as a counterpoint to another, as she belongs to a system that instilled a sense of inherent superiority and vilified nonconformity, whereas her counterpart grew up without that belief; this illustrates how circumstances and conditioning shape mindsets, which is why she garners some sympathy as those beliefs were ingrained in her from the beginning. The fourth character is similar but was open to considering alternative viewpoints and evolved progressively as she was presented with logical reasoning, rather than experiencing a sudden change in character.

Microtransactions are not going away, and only SHOULD be toned down in frequency or at the least be given a precise schedule for the repeated experience-heavy ones. Hitting the level cap on skills to access content at those levels is what most strive for and the more people at higher levels the better as it justifies more content for higher levels.
